item.title: Should you ditch Spark for DuckDB or Polars?
item.description:
Score 41 | Comments 23 (thread link) | @RobinL
December 14, 2024 | https://milescole.dev/data-engineering/2024/12/12/Should-You-Ditch-Spark-DuckDB-Polars.html | archive.org

December 12, 2024

32 minute read

There’s been a lot of excitement lately about single-machine compute engines like DuckDB and Polars. With the recent release of pure Python Notebooks in Microsoft Fabric, the excitement about these lightweight native engines has risen to a new high. Out with Spark and in with the new and cool animal-themed engines— is it time to finally migrate your small and medium workloads off of Spark?

Before writing this blog post, honestly, I couldn’t have answered with anything besides a gut feeling largely based on having a confirmation bias towards Spark. With recent folks in the community posting their own benchmarks highlighting the power of these lightweight engines, I felt it was finally time to pull up my sleeves and explore whether or not I should abandon everything I know and become a DuckDB and/or Polars convert.

While performance can be the most important driver in selecting an engine, the reality is that performance alone does not make a technology worthy of a spot in your architecture landscape. In this analysis, I’ve chosen to build a benchmark suite that aims to evaluate the following based on real-world-type test cases:

  • Performance
  • Execution Cost
  • Development Cost
  • Engine Maturity and Compatibility

The Test Cases

If I can find any complaint with benchmarks that people post, it’s that they don’t always reflect real-world use cases. The recent blog by my colleague Sandeep Pawar is fantastic, as it highlights how optimizing row group sizes can allow single-machine engines to approach V-Order-like performance. In terms of the Spark comparison, as I shared with Sandeep, the use of the LIMIT operator in his benchmark resulted in Spark running a CollectLimit operation, which forces all data on worker nodes to be collected and then filtered at the driver level. This resulted in unnecessary data movement from workers to the driver as well as a single-threaded write operation, which constrained the possible parallelism and performance. While using LIMIT to interactively return a small result set to the console is a real-world use case, returning 50M rows to the console OR using the LIMIT operation in typical ELT processes (i.e., building a fact table) is not. Therefore, it doesn’t make sense to draw serious conclusions about Spark based on this test.

For my test cases, I aimed to comprehensively cover the basic ELT use cases in a Lakehouse architecture, evaluated at both the 10GB and 100GB levels based on a sampling of TPC-DS tables generated via the Databricks DS-DGEN-based library (the largest was the store_sales table):

  1. Read Parquet, Write Delta (5x): I’ve selected five tables from the TPC-DS schema. This test simply measures the time to read the source Parquet data and write a Delta table for each of the five tables.

  2. Create Fact Table: This test measures the time to create a fact table based on the aggregation of data from the five source TPC-DS tables. A simple CREATE TABLE AS SELECT operation is run.

  3. Merge 0.1% into Fact Table (3x): This test measures the time to take a 0.1% sampling of records from the core transaction source table, join them with dimension tables, randomize values, and then merge them into the target fact table created in the prior step. This is run three times to simulate having multiple incremental loads.

  4. VACUUM (0 Hours): This measures the time to clean up old Parquet files that are no longer in the latest Delta commit. I ran with 0 hours of history retained (not recommended for production workloads) so that it would clean up the maximum number of files.

  5. OPTIMIZE: Nothing fancy about this, just the time to perform compaction.

  6. Ad-hoc Query (Small Result Aggregation): The time to perform a simple aggregated SELECT statement that returns a small result set. This imitates the type of ad-hoc query that would be run interactively and displayed for analysis.

Based on my experience consulting where I built many Lakehouse architectures, these are the types of operations that would be generally representative of end-to-end data engineering work. No APIs or semi-structured data to make things too complex—just the typical operations that would result if you had Parquet files being delivered as a starting place and the goal was to build a dimensional model to support reporting and ad-hoc queries.

Compute Configurations

I elected to use the smallest possible compute size for each respective engine for both the 10GB and 100GB benchmarks. For DuckDB and Polars, using Python Notebooks, this was the default 2-vCore VM size. For Spark, the smallest possible compute size is a Single-Node 4-vCore Spark cluster (one single Small node VM). While the starting node size for Spark is 2x bigger, Fabric Single-Node clusters allocate 50% of cores to the driver, meaning the Spark job effectively only has 2 vCores available for typical Spark tasks.

  • The 10GB benchmark was run on 2, 4, and 8-vCore machines (all single-node configurations for Spark).
  • The 100GB benchmark was run on 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32-vCore compute configurations:
    • For Spark, I used single-node configurations for 4 and 8-vCores.
    • For 16-vCores, I used a cluster with three 4-vCore worker nodes (4 driver vCores + 12 worker vCores).
    • For 32-vCores, I used a cluster with three 8-vCore worker nodes (8 driver vCores + 24 worker vCores).

For Spark, I used the Native Execution Engine (NEE), as this is a native C++ vectorized engine that makes vanilla Spark faster. There’s no additional CU rate multiplier, so there’s no reason not to use it, particularly when trying to optimize for both cost and performance.

Delta Lake Writer Configs

I used the best practice Delta Lake writer configs available in each engine.

  • For the Spark tests, I enabled deletion vectors. See my blog on this topic to understand their value.
  • For both DuckDB and Polars, since they depend on the Rust-based DeltaLake Python library, which does not support deletion vectors, this setting could not be enabled. However, at this small scale, deletion vectors only have a marginal impact on performance, so this does not skew the results in any meaningful way.

The Native Execution Engine (NEE) doesn’t yet natively support deletion vectors. When DVs are included, it results in mixed execution query plans with fallback to Spark row-based execution. Depending on the workload, DVs can still improve performance where merge-on-read results in less data being written. In this benchmark, DVs resulted in NEE completing ~3% faster.

Polars Benchmark Sampling Mod

After running the benchmark with Polars and getting OOM errors below 16-vCores, I identified that Polars does not support lazy evaluation for data sampling. This meant that to run the Merge 0.1% into Fact Table (3x) test, Polars needed to read the entire source Delta table into memory and then take an in-memory sampling of data. Spark and DuckDB, on the other hand, are able to sample directly on top of the source data, eliminating the need to load the entire table into memory.

Since sampling a large table as the source for an incremental load is not something you’d typically see in production and was only used for data generation purposes, I decided to run a second version of the benchmark for Polars. This version, labeled as Polars (Mod), uses DuckDB to perform the more efficient sampling operation (sampled_table = duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM delta_scan('abfss://...') USING SAMPLE 0.1%").record_batch()) before processing the data further with Polars.

Performance

10GB Scale

  • At 2-vCores, Polars (Mod) was the fastest engine, followed by DuckDB, and then Polars without the benchmark modification.
  • At 4-vCores, DuckDB takes the win followed by Polars and lastly Spark. DuckDB was ~1.6x faster than Spark w/ NEE.
  • At 8-vCores, DuckDB finishes only slightly faster than Spark w/ NEE. Both Polars scenarios come last.

100GB Scale

  • No engine completed the benchmark with only 2-vCores (Fabric doesn’t offer a 2-vCore node size for Spark so this wasn’t tested).
  • DuckDB was the fastest engine when using 4-vCores, taking a slight edge over Spark w/ NEE.
  • Spark w/ NEE was fastest at 8, 16, and 32-vCores.
  • Polars ran into out-of-memory (OOM) and wasn’t able to finish tests at 4 or 8 vCores. Polars was much slower than DuckDB and Spark at 16 and 32-vCores.

Note: In all of these tests, Spark has access to fewer total vCores for data processing work yet was able to keep up and even exceed the others.

Which Phases Did Different Engines Excel At?

  1. Read Parquet, Write Delta (5x)
    • 10GB: While Polars took the win at 2-vCores, DuckDB had an edge at 4-vCores.
    • 100GB: Spark was over 2x faster than both DuckDB and Polars.
  2. Create Fact Table
    • 10GB: DuckDB was ~2x faster than every other engine, with the other engines performing very similarly.
    • 100GB: DuckDB and Spark w/ NEE tied, with both Polars variants running almost 6x longer.
  3. Merge 0.1% into Fact Table (3x)
    • 10GB: Polars (Mod) was the fastest at 4-vCores, with the other engines closely clustered.
    • 100GB: Spark w/ NEE was ~2x faster than DuckDB and significantly faster than both Polars variants.
  4. VACUUM (0 Hours)
    • Neither DuckDB nor Polars have a native VACUUM command; however, the DeltaLake Python library based on Delta-rs was significantly faster than the native VACUUM command in Spark.
  5. OPTIMIZE
    • Same as VACUUM, neither DuckDB nor Polars have a native OPTIMIZE command, but the Delta-rs-based library again was significantly faster than the native OPTIMIZE command in Spark.
  6. Ad-hoc Query (Small Result Aggregation)
    • As expected, this is where engines like DuckDB and Polars provide mind-blowing, super-low-latency performance. Depending on the scale, DuckDB and Polars were between 2-6x faster than Spark w/ NEE.

10GB Results @ 4-vCores

100GB Results @ 16-vCores

Since the performance difference for VACUUM, OPTIMIZE, and Ad-hoc/Interactive Queries tends to be overshadowed by longer-running ELT processes, here’s an isolated view of the 10GB 4-vCore benchmark highlighting how much faster DuckDB and Polars (with Delta-rs) are for these workloads.

Execution Cost

Since I logged the vCores used for each run, translating to CU seconds and then the approximate dollar cost for the job was straightforward. Now that I’ve established that vanilla Spark can compete, going forward I will highlight results comparing Spark w/ NEE and deletion vectors enabled compared to DuckDB and Polars.

10GB Cost

  • Both DuckDB and Polars (Mod) were about 50% cheaper compared to Spark.
  • With 8-vCores, Spark w/ NEE and DuckDB have very close job costs ($0.019 vs $0.017).

100GB Cost

  • With 4-vCores, the DuckDB and Spark jobs cost the same at ~ $0.08.
  • With 8-vCores, the cost of the Spark job is unchanged ($0.08) but we were able to cut ~10 minutes off the processing time. Spark was the cheapest.
  • As the allocated cores increase, the relative performance gain for Spark is much higher compared to DuckDB and Polars:
    • Spark: Compared to the 4-vCore run, Spark w/ 32-vCores was 4.5x faster while the job only costs 2x more.
    • DuckDB: Compared to the 4-vCore run, DuckDB w/ 32-vCores was only 2.4x faster while the job costs 3.5x more.
    • Polars: Compared to the 16-vCore run, Polars w/ 32-vCores was only ~1.1x faster while costing ~1.9x more.

Development Cost

Selecting a compute engine isn’t just about raw performance—it’s also about how easily and quickly developers can implement solutions. In this evaluation, I focused on two key aspects of development agility: features that impact implementation time and the real-world experience of implementing this benchmark. While the feature evaluation is relatively objective, the implementation evaluation is based on my experience and prior background, making it subjective.

Key Features Impacting Development Cost

Engine SQL DataFrame API Native Delta Reader Native Delta Writer Local Development Live Monitoring Capabilities OneLake Auth Setup
Spark Yes Yes Yes Yes Poor Good but w/ a steep learning curve Excellent
DuckDB Yes No Yes No Great Poor Ok
Polars No Yes Yes Yes Great Very Poor Partial

My Analysis

  • SQL and DataFrame API: While you can use a DataFrame abstraction library like Ibis or SQLFrame, Spark is the only engine I benchmarked that natively supports both SQL and a DataFrame API. Having both presents tremendous flexibility in building data engineering pipelines. Most Spark developers I know heavily use both the SparkSQL and the DataFrame API.

  • Native Delta Writer:
    • DuckDB only supports writing to Delta tables by converting DuckDB DataFrames to another memory format and then using the DeltaLake Python library to perform the write operation. This should be natively supported in time, but today this experience of needing to convert DataFrames and use another writer was quite surprising and took some time to figure out the most optimal way to do it. I first started by converting DuckDB DataFrames to Arrow Tables via arrow() and ran into OOM issues below 16-vCore. Mim then jumped in and helped me understand that I should be using record_batch() to make this a streaming Arrow DataFrame so that the data gets processed in batches and doesn’t require the full dataset to fit into memory.
    • Polars supports a native Delta Lake writer through Delta-rs.
    • Since both DuckDB and Polars are dependent on the Delta-rs-based DeltaLake Python library for full-featured writes, both are limited by features that have yet to be implemented in Delta-rs, namely deletion vectors. This feature request was reported almost two years ago and is still open. Since deletion vectors are not supported, this means that while DuckDB can read from DV-enabled tables, since both DuckDB and Polars are dependent on Delta-rs, neither can write to such tables. See my post on deletion vectors to understand the importance of merge-on-read.

  • Local Development: DuckDB and Polars both win in the ‘local development’ category as the engines are super lightweight and can be run on a local computer with a simple PIP command. Spark is more complex, as it’s not possible to run the Fabric Spark Runtime locally. Therefore, you must connect remotely to a Fabric Spark cluster in VS Code (local or web) to get Fabric Spark-specific features. This experience is getting better every day but is not nearly as simple as running the actual engine locally.

  • Live Monitoring Capabilities: When doing development and you run something, you often might need to check to see what is actually happening. With Spark, you can look in the Spark UI or Fabric UI surfaced telemetry. It’s not perfect by any means, and the learning curve is steep, but once you have the basics figured out, it’s easy enough to check what is running, triage where something might be stuck, or evaluate live running query plans. With DuckDB, there’s a nice tqdm-style progress bar, while with Polars, you’re left to guess what might be going on and when your job might be done.

  • OneLake Auth Setup: Note, this is not a critique of the engine itself; this is an evaluation of how natively the engine is integrated to authenticate to OneLake (or ADLS) in Fabric.
    • Spark: Easy—you don’t do anything; it just works.
    • DuckDB: In hopes of avoiding more complex auth methods, I tried to get token authentication to work. I was blocked on this for a few hours until my colleague Mim Djouallah (he has some great blogs on DuckDB) saved the day and noted that I needed to upgrade to DuckDB version 1.1.3 to use this newer auth method. Once I got this one line of code, everything seamlessly works.
    • Polars: At first, I couldn’t get any Polars authentication to work, then Sandeep Pawar showed me that scan_delta() works with ABFSS paths without needing to specify auth (since it gets a token from env vars). ABFSS does not currently work with scan_parquet(), read_parquet(), and other similar methods. David Browne, however, pointed out that while ABFSS does not work for all methods, relative file paths do work: /lakehouse/default/Files since it interacts with the OneLake directory via a mount point instead of directly making ABFSS endpoint calls. I got everything working eventually, but this was frustrating to say the least.

Implementation Cost Comparison

Engine Learning Curve Implementation Speed / Workflow Integration
Spark Medium Excellent
DuckDB Medium Ok
Polars High Ok

My Analysis

  • Learning Curve

    • Spark: For myself, and I think for most people as well, learning distributed computing concepts that are critical to being successful with Spark is not a simple task. But once you get the basics, Spark is so mature that it can be hard to get too stuck. Plus, Spark supports SparkSQL, which is one of the best SQL dialects there is.

    • DuckDB: I was quite surprised how long it took me to get going with DuckDB. I couldn’t figure out how to authenticate to OneLake until Mim told me I had to update DuckDB to the latest version (1.1.3). Once I was authenticated, I was challenged by how far from straightforward it was to take my PySpark code and refactor it as DuckDB. Beyond the below challenges I stumbled through, DuckDB is almost all SQL, and thus very easy to navigate once you get going:
      • No support for natively writing to Delta tables. This includes inserts, running optimize or vacuum. You can only write to Delta tables by converting your DuckDB DataFrame to an Arrow DataFrame and then using the Delta-rs Python library to do the actual write to Delta.
      • No support for natively reading from Hive Meta Store. You can use delta_scan() or register Delta tables as views. Not hard once you understand this.
      • I originally used the arrow() method to convert DuckDB DataFrames to Arrow Tables prior to writing to Delta and experienced OOM issues. Mim thankfully showed me that the record_batch() method should be used instead so that the data is streamed into Arrow format in batches. Quite a cool feature as this allows you to run on very constrained compute and prevent OOM. That said, this was not intuitive and I have yet to find the documentation on this specific method. Is there a reason why you’d use arrow() over record_batch()? I have no idea at this point, but it seems like record_batch() makes more sense to prevent OOM.
    • Polars: Polars is a DataFrame API-centric engine, which is good news for those already comfortable with the Spark DataFrame API. That said, Polars adds additional (and possibly unnecessary?) complexity through the nuance of being able to control the evaluation model based on what methods you use. For example, read_parquet() is an eager evaluation method, while scan_parquet() is lazily evaluated. Calling the native write_delta() method to save data to a Delta table will throw an error if you chain it on top of a lazy-evaluated step, so you need to run collect() first before running write_delta() (but why can’t it just automatically do that???). Oh, and if you want to have the data be streamed for batch processing so that you can process data that is larger than your VM memory, you need to specify collect(streaming=True). I can see this level of control being fantastic if you live and breathe Polars, but this makes the learning curve pretty steep.

  • Workflow Integration / Implementation Speed: I’d define this category as how well the engine works to fit into a typical data engineering workflow. How well is it integrated into the platform? How do features of the engine impact how fast you can get work done, and do the features work with typical data engineering patterns? How complete is the engine itself, or does it feel more like a bolt-on capability?

    • Spark: I live and breathe Spark, so the actual implementation was fast for me. For the average user, I’d still suggest it can be pretty fast since things like auth, evaluation, and both reader and writer capabilities are extremely robust. Spark is a standalone, full-featured data processing engine. AL/ML, Graph, structured, semi-structured—Spark can do it all at any data size.
    • DuckDB: Ok. Could I swap some DuckDB into normal workflows? Certainly. Would I take additional time to refactor things since DuckDB doesn’t natively support Hive Meta Store and in-memory database concepts are fundamentally different? Yes. The necessity to pass DataFrames from DuckDB to the DeltaLake Writer and so forth is not hard when you get used to it, but the user experience of having to do this isn’t great and does impact the time to implement solutions.
    • Polars: Ok. The positive here is that Polars offers a native Delta Lake writer method built on Delta-rs, which provides full-featured writes (including a merge operator), and authentication for OneLake was out-of-the-box—for Delta tables. The downside is that Polars offers no SQL dialect, so you are stuck with learning a new DataFrame API and learning the nuances of having tasks evaluated with potentially both eager and lazy evaluation in the same DataFrame. This adds additional work to figure out the most optimal way to code things. That said, like DuckDB, Polars is blazing fast for querying Delta tables, and this is a big positive. I was about to give Polars an OK+ rating but will leave off the plus since I could never get Polars to complete the tests below 16-vCores, even after successfully swapping in DuckDB for the data sampling and unsuccessfully trying to improve write performance for the large table by messing with write batch sizes.

I’d easily give Spark the win in this category.

Engine Maturity and OSS Table Format Compatibility

As mentioned, the Delta-rs library which Polars is dependent on for reading Delta (DuckDB uses the Delta Kernel) and both Polars and DuckDB are dependent on for writing to Delta does not support deletion vectors. Deletion vectors are a general best practice setting for Delta tables. If you want to use Polars or DuckDB to write to Delta tables, you need to weigh the impact of not being able to use deletion vectors and potentially other newer Delta features. If your data is super small, this likely doesn’t matter, but as your data size increases, the potential impact also increases.

In terms of engine maturity, Polars and DuckDB are both relatively new. In contrast, Spark has been around for over a decade, and we are now approaching GA of the 4th major release. Spark performance continues to improve, Spark capabilities are continuing to expand, and Spark is going nowhere. Just consider some of the upcoming Spark 4.0 features:

  • Stored Procedures
  • SQL scripting constructs
  • Data Source APIs (create your own spark.read class extension)
  • Improved error logging
  • Variant data types
  • Collation support
  • Structured logging

…and so much more. All I’m trying to point out is that the Spark community is taking real action on pretty much everything that Spark doesn’t excel at or doesn’t support. In terms of performance, both Fabric and Databricks provide native C++ engines within Spark that allow Spark jobs to run much faster than natively possible with vanilla OSS Spark. Spark is here to stay and continues to improve, so get used to it. :)

New doesn’t mean bad, just that you should be cautious about APIs or syntax changes and that the engine is not going to be as full-featured as an engine like Spark that has been around for over a decade.

  • Future data growth: Avoid needing to refactor all code because your data went from small to medium and now you need to rewrite your code as PySpark. If you have small data today and a non-Spark engine only runs 2x faster, I would still use Spark simply so that I don’t have to migrate once my data gets large, as well as to take advantage of the more robust engine capabilities.

  • Skillset of team: Spark is synonymous with data processing. Tons of people know Python, more know basic SQL, but Spark supports both and since it’s been around longer, more people will have this experience. That said, I highly encourage people to learn additional languages, frameworks, and engines, so don’t rule out using DuckDB or Polars because of a potential skillset gap—just be aware there might be some time needed for cross-skilling.

  • Performance: To summarize my performance analysis, Spark can be just as fast, and even faster, for typical data engineering tasks. DuckDB and Polars can be much faster than Spark for lightweight exploration tasks and maintenance operations.

  • Cost: In my benchmark, Spark was as cheap as DuckDB and cheaper than all engines as the allocated vCores scaled. The only two tests where Spark was not the cheapest was the 10GB 2 and 4-vCore benchmarks. Remember that the cost of an engine goes beyond the direct invoice you get from your cloud provider—you should consider the cost of time to learn, the cost for your team to upskill and refactor code, and the cost of longer development cycles through the engine not being as tightly integrated as you’d like.

Ok, I’ve done the benchmark, but where would I actually use each engine now that I’ve done some basic testing and can confidently say that I’m less ignorant when it comes to single-machine engines?

If I were to optimize for performance, cost, and engine maturity/compatibility, I would do the following (with exceptions):

Primary Spark Use Cases

Any and all “data processing.” Think E.L.T., the steps to extract, load, and transform your data in the Lakehouse architecture.

Primary DuckDB Use Cases

  • Interactive and ad-hoc queries
  • Data exploration

Primary Polars Use Cases

Honestly, with DuckDB generally outperforming Polars, with zero tuning effort, and providing a rich SQL surface area, I probably wouldn’t use Polars unless there was something that DuckDB didn’t support and was significantly faster than Spark.

Primary DeltaLake Python Library Use Cases

I added this category since all of the VACUUM and OPTIMIZE operations in my benchmark for Polars and DuckDB technically were just using the DeltaLake Python library. Using a pure Python Notebook, I would use the DeltaLake library for:

  • Maintenance operations: Maintenance operations on this library were significantly faster compared to Spark. While you could use this library on a Spark cluster, there’s no need to have your worker nodes sit idle while you run lightweight jobs that only run on the driver node. Rather than running VACUUM and OPTIMIZE (where the table can fit into VM memory), I would split these maintenance jobs into a Python notebook (2-vCore for VACUUM) and have these jobs complete much faster, all while consuming much less compute.

Here’s a quick visual to summarize where I think each engine makes sense for most Lakehouse architecture use cases.

  1. Migrating off of Spark is all hype: I think the whole narrative that you should consider replacing your Spark workloads with DuckDB or Polars if your data is small is all hype. Yes, the engines have certainly earned their place at the table, however Spark is still reigns king for data processing any way you look at it. Sure, DuckDB and Polars can marginally outperform Spark at data processing at the 10GB scale on a 4-vCore (or smaller machine). I think the real story here is this:
    • Each engine does something really well, so why not strategically mix and match them to take advantage of where each truly shines. Use Spark for ELT work, use the Rust-based DeltaLake Library on Python for maintenance operations, and use DuckDB for interactive queries on your small datasets.

  2. I now have tremendous respect for Polars and DuckDB: While I prefer developing with Spark because I can move between SparkSQL and the DataFrame API as needed (without needing an abstraction library like Ibis), DuckDB’s implementation of an in-memory SQL engine is extremely powerful and could have many use cases, particularly if you don’t readily have access to use a Spark cluster.

  3. Performance with Spark more consistently scales as compute scales: I was extremely surprised to find that the performance of DuckDB and Polars was barely impacted by throwing more cores and memory at the benchmark. I’m sure there’s some magic that could be worked to tune things and get more efficient compute utilization as cores are increased, but this just isn’t something you often need to consider with Spark.

  4. Memory spill matters!: While you want to avoid it, by default, Spark can spill memory to disk if needed, making it resilient to out-of-memory (OOM) issues. With DuckDB and Polars, I ran into OOM issues (100GB @ 2-vCore for DuckDB and 2, 4, and 8-vCore for Polars), and neither engine supports memory spilling to disk to prevent the memory exhaustion causing the VM to crash. While memory spill causes Spark to run slower when it happens, it at least greatly reduces the risk of job failures and allows flexibility in compute sizing.

  5. Distributed computing has compute overhead for task orchestration, but this adds fault tolerance: When DuckDB and Polars VMs crashed due to OOM, that was it—no automatic restart or ability to resume from where it left off. The same would happen with single-node Spark clusters. However, with multi-node Spark clusters (which most production workloads use), fault tolerance is built in. If a worker node crashes for any reason, the driver node maintains the task lineage and processing state so another VM can replace the worker and resume from where the crashed VM left off, without data loss. This may lead to some in-process transformations being reprocessed, but the engine guarantees that data writes are only performed once. See my blog on RDDs vs. DataFrames for more details.

  6. Consider your specific workload: I designed my benchmark to reflect the typical lakehouse architecture that I see. Given that Spark has the biggest advantage for ELT-type data processing, if your use case involves infrequent small data loads (e.g., monthly), primarily interactive querying, or the necessity for an embedded in-memory database engine, DuckDB could be a great fit—especially for small data volumes.

Lastly, this is just another benchmark—do your own testing.

item.title: How to stop fighting with your AI pair programmer
item.description:
Score 8 | Comments 13 (thread link) | @sbpayne
December 14, 2024 | https://skylarbpayne.com/posts/cursed-cursor | archive.org

or How to Stop Fighting with your AI Pair Programmer

Cursor agent is worse than old composer.

Might go back to previous version
@ codebase

— Riley Brown (@rileybrown_ai) December 3, 2024

As someone who’s led multiple engineering teams build products from inception to international launch, I’ve seen this reaction countless times. Engineers get excited about AI coding assistants, try them out, and then… frustration. The tool seems to fight against them at every turn.

But here’s the truth I’ve learned after months of using Cursor daily while leading engineering teams and shipping production ML systems: the problem isn’t the AI. It’s how we work with it.

The Real Problem: You’re Working Solo in a Pair Programming World

Nick Dobos recently tweeted about Cursor’s agent mode:

Yoo @cursor_ai agent is CRAZY

The new ai agent mode can call arbitrary python functions in your code base!!

This means you can tell cursor agent to build its own tools!!!

“Build be a python function that can search the web”. “Now call that function to search for …” 🤯 https://t.co/gQV7qOilXu

— Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) November 27, 2024

He’s right - it is powerful. But that power is precisely why so many developers get frustrated. When you give an eager junior developer access to your entire codebase without proper guidance, what happens? The same thing that happens with Cursor’s agent mode.

As Cole Murray insightfully noted:

The people who are complaining AI sucks and doesn’t generate what they want

🤝

The people who are complaining their direct reports don’t do what they want.

Maybe you’re just bad at communicating what you want.

— cole murray (@_colemurray) December 11, 2024

In this guide, I’ll share the concrete workflow I’ve developed that transformed Cursor from a source of frustration into a genuine productivity multiplier. You’ll learn:

  • A structured approach to working with Cursor’s agent
  • How to handle both greenfield development and existing codebases
  • Complete configuration files and templates you can use today
  • Real examples from production systems

Most importantly, you’ll learn how to stop fighting with your AI pair programmer and start collaborating effectively.

The Core Problem: Communication

When using Cursor, many developers (myself included, initially) are still in a solo development mindset while technically pair programming with AI. We give one-line instructions and expect perfect implementation. Would you do that with a human teammate, particularly a junior engineer?

The solution? Treat Cursor as a teammate, not a god.

Working “Alone” Together

The irony of AI programming tools is that while they’re meant to enhance collaboration, most developers use them as if they’re still working alone. Have you ever found yourself:

# Dropping a massive chunk of code into Cursor with just:
"Fix this code"

# Or giving vague, one-line requirements like:
"Write me a function to process user data"

# Or worse, expecting it to understand complex context without explanation:
"Update this to handle the new requirements"

This approach is particularly problematic with Cursor’s agent mode, which can make sweeping changes across your codebase if not properly guided. It’s like having an eager intern with access to your entire codebase but no understanding of your team’s conventions or system architecture.

The One-Line Instruction Anti-Pattern

Let’s look at a typical interaction that leads to frustration:

Developer: "Add error handling to this function"

Cursor: *Proceeds to rewrite entire function, adding try-catch blocks everywhere, 
        changing variable names for "clarity", and introducing new helper functions*

Developer: "No, that's not what I wanted!"

Cursor: *Suggests another complete rewrite with different error handling patterns*

Developer: "F**k you Cursor!"

This pattern is especially dangerous when working with existing codebases. Cursor’s agent eagerly tries to “improve” code it sees, often breaking subtle but important patterns that aren’t immediately obvious.

Why This Fails

The failure modes become even more apparent when we compare this to human collaboration:

With a Junior Developer

You: "Here's a task. Add error handling to this function."
Junior Dev: "Okay, what kind of errors should we handle?"
You: "Good question. We need to catch network timeouts and invalid data formats."
Junior Dev: "Got it. Should we use our standard error types?"
You: "Yes, and make sure to log the errors with our logging framework."

With Cursor (Common Approach)

You: "Add error handling to this function"
Cursor: *Makes massive changes*
You: *Frustration intensifies*

The problem isn’t that Cursor is incapable - it’s that we’re not providing the same level of context and guidance we would to a human teammate.

This problem compounds when working with existing code. Consider these common scenarios:

  1. Hidden Dependencies

    # Cursor sees:
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)
   
# What it doesn't see:
# - transform() has side effects
# - Other services depend on the exact output format
# - Performance requirements that aren't obvious

  2. Implicit Patterns

    # Your codebase consistently uses:
try:
    result = risky_operation()
except SpecificError as e:
    logger.error(f"Operation failed: {e}")
    raise OperationalError(e)
   
# Cursor might introduce:
try:
    result = risky_operation()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")  # Breaking logging patterns
    return None  # Breaking error handling patterns

  3. Testing Implications

    # Cursor changes a function signature:
def process(data, config=None):  # Added optional parameter
       
# But doesn't realize this breaks:
# - Hundred of tests expecting specific behavior
# - API contracts with other services
# - Serialization/deserialization logic

The Root Cause

The fundamental issue is treating AI as a magic code generator rather than a collaborative team member. When we:

  • Skip proper requirement discussions
  • Don’t provide necessary context
  • Fail to review changes incrementally
  • Don’t explain our codebase’s patterns and constraints

We’re setting ourselves up for frustration. Just as you wouldn’t expect a new team member to write perfect code without proper onboarding, you shouldn’t expect Cursor to do so without proper guidance.

In the next section, we’ll look at a better way: a structured workflow that treats Cursor as a proper development partner rather than a god.

A Better Way: Structured Collaboration

The Four-Phase Workflow

After months of trial and error leading engineering teams through AI-assisted development, I’ve distilled our process into four key phases. This isn’t just another software development lifecycle - it’s specifically designed for effective AI collaboration while maintaining engineering rigor.

  1. Problem Statement & Requirements
    • Start with open discussion of the problem space
    • Work through expectations until you reach shared understanding
    • Document key constraints and acceptance criteria
    • Goal: Clear alignment before any code is written
  2. Design Documentation
    • Create a structured design document (I use a standard template)
    • Review and iterate on the design with Cursor
    • Break implementation into clear phases
    • Goal: Roadmap that both you and Cursor understand
  3. Phased Implementation
    • Implement solution in planned phases
    • Always reference back to the design doc
    • Regular validation against requirements
    • Goal: Manageable, reviewable chunks of work
  4. Continuous Testing
    • Follow testing strategy for each phase
    • Mix automated tests with manual validation
    • Ensure backwards compatibility
    • Goal: Confidence in changes

Key Principles

What makes this workflow effective?

  1. Small, Verifiable Steps

    # Instead of:
"Add error handling to the entire codebase"
   
# Do:
"Let's first identify the critical paths that need error handling"
"For the data processing function, what specific errors should we catch?"
"How should we integrate with our existing logging system?"

  2. Clear Context Boundaries

    # Instead of:
"Make this code better"
   
# Do:
"We need to improve error handling in process_data() to:
 1. Catch network timeouts (currently unhandled)
 2. Log errors using our standard format
 3. Maintain the existing retry behavior
 4. Keep the current function signature"

  3. Iterative Refinement

    # Instead of fighting multiple changes:
"No, not like that... no, that's not right either..."
   
# Have a dialogue:
"Good start. Let's adjust the error types to match our standards."
"Now let's add the logging integration."
"Finally, let's add the retry mechanism."

Real-World Example: Version Checksums

In the next sections, I’ll walk through a complete example of using this workflow to add version checksums to an email reply agent system. You’ll see how we:

  1. Started with a clear problem statement
  2. Developed a comprehensive design document
  3. Implemented the solution in phases
  4. Added robust testing

This wasn’t a theoretical exercise - it was a real feature we needed to prevent configuration drift in our multi-agent system. By following this structured approach, we were able to implement it correctly the first time, with no production incidents.

Initial Problem Statement

Let’s see how this workflow plays out in practice. We’ll start with discussing requirements - notice how each response builds on the previous one, creating a shared understanding.

Me: Currently, there's no way to detect if an agent's configuration has changed without a corresponding version bump. This could lead to inconsistent behavior where the same version number refers to different agent configurations. How can we detect this? Do not write code, just discuss the problem.

Cursor: You're right! There is no way to detect if an agent's configuration has changed without a corresponding version bump. We can use a checksum of the agent's configuration to detect changes. Would you like me to implement this?

Me: Let's discuss some requirements first to make sure we have the same understanding. Do not write code, just discuss the problem. First, when trying to create a new agent version which already exists, but is somehow different, we should raise an error. We don't need to get fancy and "auto update" the version number right now. The checksum should be deterministic and consistent, obviously to do this check. The check should not be performance critical; but considering most of the time is spent in the LLM inference, it is okay for it to take a little bit of time (e.g. time for a database transatction). We want to maintain backward compatibility with existing agent versions where we did not store the checksum. When there is a mismatch, we should have a clear error message. Anything else you think we should consider?

Cursor: Checksum Scope
What exactly should be included in the checksum calculation?
Should we include runtime dependencies versions?
Should we include tool implementations or just tool names?
How do we handle dynamic components (like system prompts that might depend on runtime state)?
Storage Considerations
Since we're using SQLModel, should the checksum be stored or always computed?
If stored, how do we handle migrations for existing records?
If computed, do we need indexing for efficient lookups?
3. Error Handling
Should we provide details about what changed in the error message?
Do we need different error types for different kinds of mismatches?
How do we handle validation failures during bulk operations?
Validation Timing
When exactly should we perform the validation?
Should we validate on every agent instantiation or just during version creation?
How do we handle validation in async contexts?
Debugging Support
Should we provide tools to inspect/compare checksums?
How do we help users understand why a checksum changed?
Should we log checksum computations for audit purposes?

Me: We should include runtime dependencies. Tool names are sufficient for now. No dynamic components for now, let's keep it simple. I think the checksum should be computed; because it is a derived attirbute; that makes it easier to change later, and also makes backwards compatibility simple. The data for now will be small; no indexing required. No need for now to determine what changed. In most cases, the right thing to do will be to just bump the version number. One error type should suffice. There are currently no bulk operations on agent_versions. The validation should be performed on every agent version creation. Use transactions to ensure correctness in async contexts. No need to create tools to inspect/compare checksums for now. Please summarize your understanding of the problem and requirements before we continue.

Cursor: Problem Statement:
We need to prevent silent configuration drift in agent versions. Currently, an agent's configuration could be modified without changing its version number, leading to inconsistent behavior. We need a way to detect these changes and enforce version updates.
Core Requirements:
Detect configuration changes by computing a deterministic checksum of the agent's configuration
Raise an error if trying to create an agent version that exists but has different configuration
Users should manually bump version numbers when configurations change
Technical Decisions:
Checksum includes: static configuration + tool names + runtime dependencies
Implemented as a computed property (not stored in database)
Single error type with clear message
Validation happens during agent version creation
Use database transactions for async safety
Keep implementation simple (no inspection tools, bulk operations, or change detection)
Non-Requirements (for now):
No automatic version bumping
No dynamic components in checksum
No tool implementation checksums
No inspection/comparison tools
No indexing for checksums
No detailed change detection

While this might seem like a lot of detail upfront – it’s all important stuff to make sure Cursor is going to do the right thing! Now let’s make a design doc!

Design Document

Me: Let's create a design document given the problem statement and requirements we discussed. Please write a markdown file following the @context/design_doc.md template.

And Cursor drops this gold on us:

# Agent Version Checksum Feature

## Problem Statement

We need to prevent silent configuration drift in agent versions. When an agent's 
configuration is modified without changing its version number, it can lead to:

- Inconsistent behavior between environments
- Hard to debug issues
- Loss of reproducibility
- Untracked configuration changes

## Requirements

### Functional Requirements

- Compute deterministic checksum of agent configuration
- Validate configuration matches when creating agent versions
- Raise error if version exists with different configuration
- Support existing agent versions (backward compatibility)

### Non-Functional Requirements

- Performance: Can tolerate database transaction overhead
- Clear error messages directing users to bump version
- Simple implementation (single error type)
- Safe operation in async contexts

## Design Decisions

### 1. Checksum Storage

Implemented as computed field because:

- Easier to modify checksum logic later
- Simplifies backward compatibility
- Keeps data model clean
- Reflects derived nature of the field

### 2. Checksum Algorithm

Uses SHA-256 because:

- Cryptographically secure (prevents accidental collisions)
- Standard library implementation available
- Fast computation
- Widely used and trusted

### 3. Configuration Serialization

Uses deterministic JSON serialization because:

- Handles nested configurations naturally
- Human-readable for debugging
- Consistent across Python versions
- Supports all needed data types

### 4. Checksum Scope

Includes in computation:

- Static configuration
- Tool names (not implementations)
- Runtime dependencies

Excludes:

- Dynamic components
- Tool implementations
- Runtime state

## Technical Design

### 1. Core Components

```python
class AgentVersion:
    """Stores and validates agent version information"""
    version: str
    checksum: str
    
    def validate_checksum(self, config: AgentConfig) -> bool:
        """Validates configuration matches stored checksum"""
        return self.checksum == compute_checksum(config)

def compute_checksum(config: AgentConfig) -> str:
    """Generates deterministic checksum from configuration"""
    serialized = json.dumps(config.dict(), sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()
```

### 2. Integration Points

- AgentVersion integrates with InstrumentedAgent creation
- Validation occurs during agent initialization
- Checksum computation hooks into configuration serialization
- Error handling integrates with agent creation workflow

## Implementation Plan

1. Phase 1: Core Implementation (Completed)
   - Added checksum field to AgentVersion
   - Implemented checksum computation
   - Added validation logic
   - Created error types

2. Phase 2: Migration (Completed)
   - Updated existing agent configurations
   - Added validation to agent creation
   - Updated tests
   - Added documentation

## Testing Strategy

### Unit Tests

- Checksum computation consistency
- Version validation logic
- Configuration change detection
- Error case handling

### Integration Tests

- Agent creation workflow
- Configuration updates
- Version management
- Migration scenarios

## Observability

### Logging

- Configuration validation results
- Checksum computation details
- Version mismatch events
- Migration progress

### Metrics

- Validation failures
- Configuration changes
- Version updates
- Migration status

## Future Considerations

### Potential Enhancements

- Version comparison operations
- Configuration drift detection
- Automated version bumping
- Checksum verification tools

### Known Limitations

- Only detects changes in serializable fields
- Requires manual version management
- No partial configuration updates
- Limited to JSON-serializable types

## Dependencies

### Runtime Dependencies

- Python standard library (json, hashlib)
- Existing agent configuration system
- Version management system

### Development Dependencies

- Testing framework
- JSON schema validation
- Development documentation

## Security Considerations

- Checksum algorithm is cryptographically secure
- No sensitive data in checksums
- Version records are immutable
- Validation prevents configuration tampering

## Rollout Strategy

1. Development phase (Completed)
   - Core implementation
   - Test coverage
   - Documentation

2. Testing phase (Completed)
   - Unit tests
   - Integration tests
   - Migration testing

3. Production deployment (Completed)
   - Gradual rollout
   - Migration support
   - Monitoring

## References

- Original design document
- Agent configuration documentation
- Version management system documentation
- SHA-256 specification

This design document gives us clear boundaries for implementation while remaining flexible enough for iteration. Note how it includes concrete interfaces and clear phase definitions. I can hear you already: “BuT cUrSoR hAlLuCiNaTeS!” Totally! And that’s why we need to review and verify the work. We are FORCING Cursor to output enough information so that we can verify. How closely you pay attention to certain details is mostly a function of your risk tolerance. Everything you do not carefully verify is something that could be wrong – just like with a human teammate you are mentoring! Not meant as a slight to the human teammate, they are learning; everyone has to start somewhere.

I like this design, except that it isn’t properly using SQLModel as it should, let’s remind Cursor of that for the interfaces:

Me: Let's amend this design document. Keep in mind we should be using SQLModel for storage of the fields. I think we should use `@hybrid_property` from SQLAlchemy to make it storable in the database.

And it updated the interface to this (looks good to me):

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Stores and validates agent version information"""
    # Primary key fields
    agent_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    
    # Metadata
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    
    # Configuration fields (stored as JSON)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))
    
    @hybrid_property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum from static fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
            "runtime_info": self.runtime_info,
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()

One thing I’ll admit here: this wasn’t entirely generated by Cursor. I made one hand edit. And that’s okay! I added the sorted(self.tools) to ensure the order of tools is consistent. This was easier to do myself than explain to the AI.

Now we have a good looking design doc, let’s move on to the implementation!

Implementation and Testing

Now, we are all familiar with the cyclic and iterative nature of implementation and testing. You try something, it doesn’t work, you try something else. Rinse and repeat. It’s no different here! Let’s start with the first phase of implementation and testing. Remember: we ALWAYS refer to back to the previous step to “ground” Cursor.

Me: Please implement the first phase of @design/agent_version_checksum.md.

Cursor then starts by creating a new branch:

git checkout -b feature/agent-version-checksum-phase-1

And then Cursor excitedly starts writing code. It’s challenging to show all the code that was written because some were edits, but suffice to say: Cursor was pretty damn close to the design document. The key implementation in phase 1 was this:

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Captures the complete configuration of an agent at a point in time."""

    __table__: ClassVar[Table]

    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    agent_id: str = Field(index=True)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))

    @hybrid_property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum of static configuration fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()
   
   def validate_configuration(self, agent_config: "AgentConfig") -> None:
        """Validate that an agent config matches this version's configuration.
        
        Args:
            agent_config: The configuration to validate
            
        Raises:
            ConfigurationError: If the configuration doesn't match this version
        """
        # Convert agent config to comparable format
        config_prompt = [agent_config.system_prompt]
        config_tools = sorted(getattr(agent_config, 'tools', []))
        
        check_fields = {
            "prompt_template": config_prompt,
            "tools": config_tools,
        }
        
        check_sum = hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(check_fields, sort_keys=True).encode()
        ).hexdigest()
        
        if check_sum != self.checksum:
            raise ConfigurationError(
                f"Configuration mismatch for version {self.version_id}. "
                f"Expected checksum {self.checksum}, got {check_sum}. "
                "Did you forget to bump the version number?"
            )

I generally like to start with a sort of manual e2e test when I am working on smaller projects.

Me: Please run the agent to ensure nothing is broken.

Cursor suggests running the following: uv run -m email_reply_agent.gmail_agent And we quickly find that the agent is broken!

pydantic.errors.PydanticUserError: A non-annotated attribute was detected: `checksum = <sqlalchemy.ext.hybrid.hybrid_property object at 0x1058058d0>`. All model fields require a type annotation; if `checksum` is not meant to be a field, you may be able to resolve this error by annotating it as a `ClassVar` or updating `model_config['ignored_types']`.

It appears that the agent is broken, and it has something to do with the new checksum attribute. As most people do, we pipe that error back to Cursor, Cursor makes another edit, and then we run the agent again… Same error! Now here is where we usually get frustrated, Cursor obviously is stuck and does not know what to do. Cursor is a nervous intern! They don’t want to admit they don’t know; we need to help by providing context.

A quick Google search from me shows that @hybrid_property is not the way to use a computed field in SQLModel (oopsie my bad), instead we should use @computed_field! I provide that as context, using Hamel’s awesome chrome extension to convert a webpage to markdown. I also told Cursor I didn’t like having a “validate” method in the class and would prefer inlining the comparison, and Cursor made the change:

class AgentVersion(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Captures the complete configuration of an agent at a point in time."""

    # Use SQLAlchemy Table for proper table configuration
    __table__: ClassVar[Table]

    agent_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    version_id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    prompt_template: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    tools: list[str] = Field(default=[], sa_column=Column(JSON))
    runtime_info: dict[str, str] = Field(default={}, sa_column=Column(JSON))

    @computed_field
    @property
    def checksum(self) -> str:
        """Compute checksum from static fields."""
        static_fields = {
            "prompt_template": self.prompt_template,
            "tools": sorted(self.tools),
            "runtime_info": self.runtime_info,
        }
        serialized = json.dumps(static_fields, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode()).hexdigest()

    class Config: # type: ignore  # noqa: PGH003
        table = True
        arbitrary_types_allowed = True

    # Set table name after class definition
    __tablename__ = "agent_versions" # type: ignore  # noqa: PGH003

...

async def store_version(self, version: AgentVersion) -> None:
        """Store an agent version if it doesn't exist.

        Args:
            version: The version to store

        Raises:
            ConfigurationError: If version exists with different configuration
        """
        async with self.db.session() as session:
            # Check if version exists
            stmt = select(AgentVersion).where(
                and_(
                    AgentVersion.agent_id == version.agent_id,
                    AgentVersion.version_id == version.version_id,
                )
            )
            existing = await session.execute(stmt)
            existing_version = existing.scalar_one_or_none()

            if existing_version is not None:
                if existing_version.checksum != version.checksum:
                    raise ConfigurationError(  # noqa: TRY003
                        f"Configuration mismatch for agent {version.agent_id} "
                        f"version {version.version_id}. "
                        "The configuration has changed without a version bump."
                    )
                return  # Version exists and matches

            session.add(version)
            await session.commit()

And this code worked! It ran successfully the first time, then when I changed the config without the version, it failed!

Then we ask Cursor to write a few unit tests to ensure the checksum is computed correctly:

Me: Okay, the manual run is working. Now let's write a few unit tests to ensure the checksum is computed correctly.

Cursor writes a few unit tests, and we run them to ensure they pass:

"""Tests for agent version checksum functionality."""
import pytest
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlmodel import SQLModel

from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.models import AgentVersion
from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.storage import SQLModelStorage, ConfigurationError


@pytest.fixture
async def db_session():
    """Create a test database session."""
    engine = create_async_engine(
        "sqlite+aiosqlite:///test.db",
        echo=False,
    )
    
    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)
    
    async_session = sessionmaker(
        engine, class_=AsyncSession, expire_on_commit=False
    )
    
    async with async_session() as session:
        yield session
        await session.rollback()
    
    await engine.dispose()


@pytest.fixture
def storage(db_session):
    """Create a test storage instance."""
    return SQLModelStorage(db_session)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_checksum_computation():
    """Test that checksum is computed correctly."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # Same config should have same checksum
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum == version2.checksum

    # Different config should have different checksum
    version3 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    assert version.checksum != version3.checksum


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_storage_validation(storage):
    """Test that version storage validates checksums."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # First store should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Same version should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Different config with same version should fail
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    with pytest.raises(ConfigurationError):
        await storage.store_version(version2)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_order_independence():
    """Test that checksum is independent of field order."""
    version1 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9", "os": "linux"}
    )
    
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool2", "tool1"],  # Different order
        runtime_info={"os": "linux", "python": "3.9"}  # Different order
    )
    
    assert version1.checksum == version2.checksum

uv run pytest tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py

But we find a failure:

================================================================================= short test summary info =================================================================================
ERROR tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py::test_version_storage_validation - AttributeError: 'async_generator' object has no attribute 'database_url'
========================================================================= 2 passed, 2 warnings, 1 error in 0.13s ==========================================================================

So we tell Cursor to fix the test. Key insight here: don’t just jump into fixing the test, but instead think about and discuss the problem with me!

Me: One test failed with: ERROR tests/test_agent_version_checksum.py::test_version_storage_validation - AttributeError: 'async_generator' object has no attribute 'database_url'. Please discuss the problem and how you think we can fix it. Do not write code.

Cursor: Ah, I see the issue. The problem is with our test fixture setup. The storage fixture is receiving the session directly, but SQLModelStorage expects a database configuration object with a session factory method. Would you like me to fix the test?

Me: Yes, that sounds right, please proceed! Make a separate SQLModelConfig fixture that we can use to configure and setup the database.

Then Cursor makes a fix:

"""Tests for agent version checksum functionality."""
import pytest
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlmodel import SQLModel

from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.models import AgentVersion
from email_reply_agent.agent_instrumentation.db.storage import ConfigurationError, SQLModelConfig, SQLModelStorage


@pytest.fixture
def storage_config():

async def setup_database(storage_config):
    """Set up and tear down the test database."""
    print("Setting up database:", storage_config.database_url)
    engine = create_async_engine(
        storage_config.database_url,
        echo=False
    )

    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        print("Creating all tables:", SQLModel.metadata.tables)
        await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)


@pytest.fixture
def storage(storage_config):
    """Create a test storage instance."""
    return SQLModelStorage(storage_config)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_checksum_computation():
    """Test that checksum is computed correctly."""
    version = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Test prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    # Same config should have same checksum
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",

        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}

    assert version.checksum == version2.checksum

    # Different config should have different checksum
    version3 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",

    assert version.checksum != version3.checksum

    """Test that version storage validates checksums."""
    await setup_database(storage_config)

    # First store should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Same version should succeed
    await storage.store_version(version)
    
    # Different config with same version should fail
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",
        prompt_template=["Different prompt"],
        tools=["tool1", "tool2"],
        runtime_info={"python": "3.9"}
    )
    
    with pytest.raises(ConfigurationError):
        await storage.store_version(version2)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_version_order_independence():
    """Test that checksum is independent of field order."""
    version1 = AgentVersion(

    )
    
    version2 = AgentVersion(
        agent_id="test_agent",
        version_id="0.0.1",

    )
    
    assert version1.checksum == version2.checksum

Now I am pretty happy with the implementation and the tests pass. One thing that bothers me is that the test.db is not cleaned up here:

Me: Please make sure in @test_agent_version_checksum.py that we clean up the database in between test runs.

Cursor makes a fix and now the tests pass and the database is cleaned up! I’m pretty happy:

class TestDatabase:
    """Context manager for test database setup and cleanup."""
    
    def __init__(self, config: SQLModelConfig):
        self.config = config
        self.engine = create_async_engine(config.database_url, echo=False)
    
    async def __aenter__(self):
        """Create database tables."""
        async with self.engine.begin() as conn:
            await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.create_all)
    
    async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        """Drop database tables and cleanup."""
        async with self.engine.begin() as conn:
            await conn.run_sync(SQLModel.metadata.drop_all)
        await self.engine.dispose()

# ... then in tests

async with TestDatabase(storage_config):
   ...


Me: Please make a PR for the first phase of @design/agent_version_checksum.md.

Cursor runs the following commands:

git add .
git commit -m "First phase of agent version checksum"
gh pr create --title "First phase of agent version checksum" --body "First phase of agent version checksum"

And I can then go review the PR, and merge it!

Best Practices

Now that we have gone through a full cycle of this workflow, I want to extract out what I have found to be best practices.

  • Enforce an opinionated development workflow on Cursor: the specific workflow I went through is not necessarily a best practice; it’s that I went through a workflow that’s the highest leverage. Adapt to your own setting as needed!
  • Focus on collaboration and communication before code: Cursor (and sometimes we) are so eager to jump into code. But before we really understand that’s a mistake! Give explicit “Do not write code” directives.
  • Always force Cursor to use the context of the previous step: this helps ground Cursor to the most recent item you agreed on. It’s important to “attach” the resource to the context of your conversation too. Because you may have made edits Cursor didn’t see!
  • Limit the Size of Each Step: don’t give Cursor too much to chew on at once. This is a great way to get stuck in a loop. Instead, give them smaller chunks (this is why I split up the design doc into phases).
  • Guide the Discussion: without guardrails, Cursor will… well go off the rails. Make sure to keep Cursor on track. Don’t be afraid to “cancel” Cursor and reset.
  • Return to the Previous Step if Needed: sometimes Cursor will seem hopelessly stuck in a loop. Don’t keep going forward; go backwards. It is clear that Cursor is missing (or misunderstanding) some critical context; discuss what that is before proceeding (and make according edits to artifacts like design docs)!
  • Document Everything: Force Cursor (and yourself) to leave breadcrumbs. This will help you pick up where you left off and be critical for you, Cursor, and possibly other teammates to understand what’s going on!

Tips for Applying in Teams

Engineering leaders constantly tell me: “oh I can use Cursor because I know what I’m doing, but the junior engineers really can’t use it effectively”. I think this is bullshit. The reality is that this is a tool like any other, and it is the responsibility of senior engineers / leaders to teach juniors how to use their tools effectively. AI does not let senior engineers off the hook for mentoring their juniors. And we also should be cautious about giving junior engineers too much for them to chew.

Here is what I found worked best:

  • Give smaller chunks: instead of giving a junior the entire project from the start, do the first few steps with them. Then you can hand off a design doc and let them take a stab at implementing whatever “phase 1” is.
  • Review intermediate phases: if you give a junior a design doc, you should review their implementation of the first phase. This will help you understand their level of understanding and give you a chance to guide them. But you could also give them the entire project upfront and review each step – e.g. review the problem statement / requirements upfront. This can be an incredible way to help them grow!
  • Give more complex tasks as they grow: as the junior grows, you can increase the complexity of what you give them (and of what you let them do).
  • Regularly pair with them: I have never found a good substitute for sitting down and pairing with them; you get a lot of insight into how they think and what may unlock their growth.

From Fighting to Flow: Making AI Work For You

When I started working with AI coding tools, I experienced the same frustrations you might be feeling now. But after leading multiple teams to successfully integrate these tools into their workflows, I’ve seen firsthand how transformative they can be when used effectively.

The key shift? Stop treating AI as a code generation oracle and start treating it as a collaborative team member. The workflow I’ve shared isn’t just theory – it’s battle-tested across multiple international product launches and production ML systems.

Remember:

  • A structured workflow beats raw capability
  • Clear communication prevents most problems
  • Small, focused steps lead to better outcomes
  • Teams grow stronger when given the right framework

Ready to Transform Your AI Development?

If you want to dive deeper:

  • Check out my Cursor setup guide for technical configuration
  • Connect with me on LinkedIn to discuss AI development practices
  • Follow me on X for daily insights on effective AI collaboration
  • Schedule a consultation if you need help building an AI-powered development workflow for your team

Most importantly, start small. Pick one project, apply this workflow, and adjust it to your needs. You’ll be surprised how quickly fighting with your AI assistant turns into flowing with a capable teammate.

Share your experiences with me on X or LinkedIn – I’d love to hear how this workflow works for you and what you’ve learned along the way.
